sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: One of our teammates had to sit out of Taekwondo Nationals due to a strain injury. The cause? A rushed 5-minute warm-up that just wasn’t enough. It was a harsh reminder: skimping on warm-ups (Even if it's boring) is a common mistake, but it leads to real consequences...injury, lost training time, and missed opportunities. It's also a great way for people to get active and stay healthy!

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: We set out to turn that mundane yet critical step into something athletes actually look forward to: an interactive AR warm-up game. By combining guided drills, live feedback, and playful challenges, our system makes proper warm-ups engaging, adaptive, and fun—so athletes are ready to perform and stay safe. Once you put on our glasses and wear our helmet, Coach Bob will shout playful insults to encourage you to get into shape and warm up! He'll also highlight with coloured nodes on the punching bag from the AR glasses whether to do a kick, knee, hook, jab, or straight to the head or body to add variance to the routine. Lastly, performance data such as speed, force, and time are all relayed onto a dashboard which can be viewed after warming up. (Keep in mind that frame rate is much smoother when wearing glasses and not streaming the live feed!)

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Used XReal1 glasses to project targets onto Bob with open CV Used OAK 1 AF Camera to get first person footage Used Gemini and Eleven Labs to give Coach Bob a voice Used a MPU-6050 and Bob's wobbles after impact to calculate force of hits and to register them Pulled everything together :)

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: We ran into a few big challenges during the build. Since we started later than most teams, we didn’t have specialized sensors to log hit force, so we had to get creative with how we handled impact registration using only the materials we had on hand. On top of that, the AR experience initially suffered from lag and jitter, which meant we had to spend extra time refining performance and smoothing out visuals to keep it engaging. Finally, because the setup would be actively struck and moved around, we had to reinforce and secure all the hardware to make sure it stayed intact during real use.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We’re proud that, despite starting later than other teams, we delivered a working AR warm-up game that athletes actually enjoyed using!

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: NEVER GIVE UP! PLEASE WARM UP BEFORE TRAINING! In the future we want to build a robust teaching feature which can hopefully help people sharpen their martial arts techniques! (Also a multiplayer mode / leaderboard).

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Stock Lock bridges the gap between people and traditional stock market analysis with AI-powered, real-time investment insights. By leveraging real-time market data from Yahoo Finance and Gemini, along with cutting-edge AI models like RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), we aimed to create a system that doesn't just predict stock prices but helps users understand market trends and make data-driven investment decisions.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Our Stock Lock is designed to provide real-time stock market insights and predictions. It pulls live data from trusted sources like the Yahoo Finance API and Gemini API, offering up-to-date information on stock prices and market trends. By using a combination of advanced AI models, including a RAG model and LSTM networks, the application analyzes historical stock data and performs time series analysis to predict future stock prices based on user input. Users can interact with the tool by entering a stock ticker, and the system will provide predictions on future stock prices. This allows users to make more informed decisions about their investments. Additionally, our model can generate insights about the overall market and specific stocks, creating a more personalized and data-driven approach to investing.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The core backend of our application is based on an LSTM model through TensorFlow. The data fed into the model is collected through an API call from Yahoo Finance to get real-time data for increased accuracy. We used other Python libraries such as LangChain, Matplotlib, Numpy, and Pandas in order to develop the RAG model and preprocess the data for the neural network. The frontend was developed using Streamlit.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The training of our LSTM model was challenging due to the complex structure of the neural network. Retrieving and training the data in the context of finance was also a challenge. It was our first time working with a RAG model, and learning vector database concepts was challenging.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

We were able to successfully implement the LSTM model, taking time series analysis into consideration to make our predictions. We were able to train our LLM with specific context in order to avoid hallucinations.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned the importance of data preprocessing and how it hugely impacts the accuracy of the machine learning model through our trial-and-error process. We also learned how to add context to the RAG model to get specific information from the LLM.

sections.heading: What's next for Stock Lock
sections.text: Stock Lock will soon be able to integrate as an extension to your stock portfolio, providing real-time pop-up suggestions while you are investing. It will also be scaled into a subscription-based stock advising application.

devpost_page.title: Luyten
devpost_page.tagline: An agentic finance ERP where AI agents do the month-end close but requires approval before postage: a Red Team critiques, an Advisor rules, and the CFO confirms.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: At a growing startup, the month-end close still takes the finance team about ten days. Most of that time goes to matching deposits to invoices, chasing receipts and rebuilding revenue schedules in spreadsheets. Agents could already do most of this work. But ask a CFO whether they'd let a model post straight to the general ledger and the answer is no, because nobody can see what the agent did or stop it before it lands. We wanted agents that do the work and still can't change the books on their own.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Luyten is automated finance for 10x growth startups , built first for SaaS companies. Agents run the month-end close for a group of companies in two currencies, and every change passes through a gate: Worker agents propose. Bookkeeper, Revenue, Credit & Risk and Consolidation create Proposals. None of them can post. The Red Team critiques. It runs on models the workers don't use: Grok goes first, then Gemini adds what Grok missed. The Advisor rules. It approves, amends or rejects each Proposal and writes down why. The CFO confirms anything material. Anything at or above the $10,000 Materiality threshold, and every amendment, waits in the Needs your OK queue until the CFO confirms it with one click or sends it back. Before money moves, Credit & Risk checks the people behind each customer and vendor. It runs identity, fraud, all three credit bureaus and public records through the CRS Credit API, and Bright Data collects their public footprint. The database derives the Risk Tier from those facts, and the tier sets payment terms. Each agent follows a plain-English Charter, which the finance team can tighten but never loosen. Every number in the Board Pack drills down to its journal lines, then to the Proposal, then to the agent debate behind it. Luyten also runs as an agent on Fetch.ai's Agentverse, so you can ask the Advisor how the business is doing from ASI:One.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: SpacetimeDB is the whole backend : the ledger, the approval queue, the audit trail and the message bus between agents. The SvelteKit app subscribes to it and updates as rows change. Each agent role connects with its own identity, and every reducer checks who is calling, so the approval gate lives in the database and not in a prompt. The CFO seat is claimed once with a one-time secret. The bank feed has its own identity, and all it can do is add raw bank lines and invoices. The accounting runs in a pure double-entry engine that stores money as 64-bit integer minor units. The database recomputes what matters before anything posts: consolidation entries are rebuilt from the books, and credit tiers come from the recorded facts, never from the agent. The workers and the Advisor run on the Claude Agent SDK , and a local bridge can send the same calls to OpenAI. The Red Team runs on Grok and Gemini through the Vercel AI SDK , and Credit & Risk runs its cascade against the CRS sandbox over MCP . Every external provider has a recorded stand-in. The full demo runs with no API keys, through the same identities and reducers as a live run.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest product question was what a startup CFO would open this app for between closes. An automated close is useful once a month, but a CFO also watches runway, burn, margin and the next raise, so we had to decide which features earned a place beyond the close. We chose a dashboard for cash, burn, runway, ARR and churn, a cost-of-service view for gross margin, and views for financing and payroll. Agent communication was the other hard part. Getting six agents on three model vendors to propose, critique, rule and escalate in order meant defining one Proposal format that every agent reads and writes, and sending every message through the database.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A rogue agent can't write to the books, and our tests prove it. On every pull request, CI runs the module smoke test, which tries every gate and refusal against a real SpacetimeDB. 156 ledger engine unit tests (1,085 across the workspace), and the CRS cascade reproduces all 20 decisions in the sandbox dataset. One click starts the close for a two-company group. That close produces 52 Proposals, catches a duplicate payment, and blocks two vendors before their first payment: one owner is a synthetic identity and the other is deceased. Real financial analysis beyond the close. The consolidated Board Pack has the P&L, balance sheet, ARR waterfall and NRR. The dashboard tracks cash, burn, runway, DSO, churn and gross margin by cost of service, and every figure drills down to its journal lines. An interface for two kinds of reader: a founder who wants the one-sentence summary on each Proposal, and a controller who wants the journal lines underneath.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: SpacetimeDB turned out to be far more than a database. Its reducers became our permission layer and its identities became our agent roles. Its subscriptions gave us a live UI and an audit trail without writing a separate backend. We also learned that agents work better when they communicate in structure. Agents that hand each other typed Proposals and written rationales are easier to debug, test and trust than agents chatting freely. And putting a second model vendor in the critic's seat caught mistakes the first model had agreed with.

sections.heading: What's next for Luyten
sections.text: First comes an Intake agent that reads the payables inbox, Stripe and bank accounts through read-only connectors. It writes through the same ingest-only role as today's feed. A hijacked Intake agent could add evidence but couldn't propose, rule or post. After that come per-company locks and hosted instances for a handful of SaaS design partners, and we'll widen the rollout as the Charter evals show each agent is reliable. For customers, the payoff is a close that takes days instead of weeks, a smaller finance team, fraud and credit risk caught earlier, and books that are ready for audit at any point. Longer term, those audited books become leverage: Luyten will use them to negotiate working-capital terms for its customers, with the CFO confirming every offer through the same gate.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Projects & Nodes – Each film is a project with a tree of nodes (logline, characters, objects, scenes, final film). Editing a parent marks descendants as stale so they regenerate with fresh context. Only required context is passed when generating each node. Generation Jobs – Every AI action (LLM plot, character sheet, image, video, final stitch) is a generation, queued as a job in Redis. Artifacts – JSON descriptors, images, frame stills, scene clips, and the stitched film are all stored as downloadable artifacts in blob storage.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We wanted to visualize a neural network with circuitry. Initially, we wanted to build a physical neural network (PNN) that conducts computations using conductance and resistance, with inspiration from https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03372 . However, we pivoted to modeling a neural network using LEDs similar to The Stillwell Brain by Vsauce.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: The CwNN classifies a drawn digit on the computer and lights up the corresponding activated neurons in the LED neural network. Layers are color-coded, and users can hover over activated neurons in specific layers to see which neurons in the previous layers caused it to activate. This enables users to visualize the process of a neural network better.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The CwNN was built using LED strips that were soldered together, an Arduino UNO, and JavaScript for the frontend.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: It was difficult working with hardware because our team had little experience with circuitry. Additionally, indexing the LEDs was tedious since there were hundreds of LEDs.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to send data from the computer to the Arduino and how to model a neural network with only discrete weights.

sections.heading: What's next for Circuitry with Neural Networks
sections.text: We would like to implement CwNNs with back propagation and to train our own neural network. Additionally, instead of visualizing a neural network, we would like to implement a physical neural network through current.

I often went shopping for ingredients at nearly every meal since they had to be constantly restocked in my small pantry(space under bed)/(quarter of a mini)fridge, I had to lug around all of my ingredients and utensils to the nearby lounges looking for an unoccupied one, I had to wash dishes one at a time since there was no place to put wet dishes. This naturally prompted me to seek out partners to cook with, but I often found that friends were busy and reaching out to people on instagram wasted even more time.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Husky Dormers allows prospective cooks or just anyone looking to gather people for a purpose to plan an event. It was built with delegating cooking tasks between people, as a sort of team up so everyone gets a meal and they spend less time. It also serves as a general event planner than people can use to advertise or organize hangouts. The driving motivation is connecting students conveniently.

sections.heading: How we built it

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into

We had to look into each resource and decide as a team what technology would be practical for us to use and truly be necessary to see our idea to fruition. One example is Drizzle, which remnants of are still whispered about in our code. At the start, we added it to the project, but as time went on, we eventually realized that it was not necessary to our project and abandoned it.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of

devpost_page.title: Ink Habitat
devpost_page.tagline: Draw your creature and watch it come to life!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were inspired by the farm-related games we've played before. It is a pity that we couldn't create our own creatures because there were some restrictions on the creatures in the game shops – sometimes, they didn't look the way we wanted, and it was boring. So, we asked ourselves why not draw our own creatures. At first, we designed the Grasslands island to be the base world of our game and started drawing our creatures. But after some time we understood that it is a bit dull when you only draw your creatures and watch how they move. And then, we invented the friend system and battles between friends – so that you could go to your friend's farm and battle with them and get one of their creatures.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Ink Habitat is a creature farm where you can draw your creatures, give them names and speech, assign them unique behaviour and voices with AI(Gemini and ElevenLabs), and bring them to life in a virtual environment. You will get an opportunity to explore different landscapes such as Grassland, Desert, and Ocean, visit your friends' farms, and fight them in creature team battles using three creatures. Each battle includes random buff cards that may be helpful or detrimental to your creatures. In order to increase the realism of the game, all creatures that took part in the battle must have some rest after it.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We started by sketching the basic island environment and designing our own creatures. We then built the website and developed the different features step by step, including creature creation, farm exploration, friend interactions, and the battle system. We also integrated AI into the project to help bring our hand-drawn creatures to life with animations and attack behaviours, along with voice clips that make each creature feel more unique. We used GitHub to manage our code and collaborate throughout development.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The most difficult part was designing the battle mechanics. After adding random buff cards to our game, the process of balancing became even more challenging. It was necessary to consider how one card or another would affect the player’s team of creatures.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Neither of us had experience in game-making before, so creating Ink Habitat became quite a challenge for both of us. In the beginning, we had an easier task in mind that we were more familiar with. But we have chosen to leave our comfort zone and create something unique and innovative. What we are really proud of is that we managed to create an interactive world of creatures with custom-made drawings, different locations, social interactions, and battles. What is even more important, we did not choose the easy way out.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: During the hackathon, we acquired some skills in working with GitHub in terms of collaboration, making changes in the code and integrating various parts of the project. Also, we've understood how we could use AI to our advantage and make our creatures interactive without creating all the animations manually. Moreover, we've realized that game development is not only about developing the concept. Sometimes even something simple may turn out to be quite complex.

sections.heading: What's next for Ink Habitat
sections.text: In the future, we plan to make our creatures more interactive, as opposed to just clicking on them to see how they move. Instead, the players will be able to give food to the creatures, train them, level them up, and establish more bonds with them. In addition, it would be interesting to consider ways to enable the creatures to move from the website to the players' computer screens as their little virtual companions. We would like for our Ink Habitat to be more of a world to live and grow in, rather than a game which people only play.

devpost_page.title: Ripple
devpost_page.tagline: Intelligently model the effects of infrastructure collapse on local neighborhoods and visualize the impact of prospective city planning.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: American public transport has a reputation of being quite poor: Constant delays, the massive car culture, and a general lack of infrastructure are all common problems. Despite this, many people are entirely dependent on it. This systemically underrepresented group is hit the hardest when disasters strike, being denied access to key utilities like healthcare or groceries. As Georgia Tech students, we’re right in the middle of Atlanta, so HackGT felt like the perfect opportunity to look at just how vulnerable and critical public transport is to the people who rely on it. Thus, we decided our project would focus on visualizing the impact of failing infrastructure on Atlanta.

sections.heading: Building the system
sections.text: We started with a simple goal: Get a map of Atlanta, put MARTA into it, and see who and what gets affected by it. For the map, we found LibreMap was a great library that provided a high level of detail and geographical accuracy. From there, we had to figure out how we wanted to store the data. One of the sponsors, TigerData, interested us since it was a new type of software that we hadn’t played with before. We implemented PostgreSQL to store a) a graph representation of the MARTA train stations, b) regions of households based on ZIP code, and c) points of interest that people go to every day. Specifically, these are high-impact locations like hospitals, clinics, and grocery stores that people need to go to every day to survive. We found this data from the MARTA GTFS, the U.S. Census, and OpenStreetMap. Putting data into the database was helpful for aggregating different data sources into one database. We rendered this data onto the map with Deck.gl , finishing our visualization. However, now came the hard part of seeing how critical infrastructure closing impacted people’s everyday lives. For that, we developed a unique simulation algorithm: We trained a statistical model to figure out what points of interest (hospitals, grocery stores, libraries, etc., POIs for short) people went to every day and at what frequency based on their location. To train this, we used data from OpenStreetMap and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Then, we established the nearest POIs to

sections.heading: Making the simulation realistic
sections.text: This algorithm didn’t work immediately though. We ran into some challenges. Originally, we used absolute distance to detect which places were nearest to each housing region. This made our data completely unrepresentative of reality. Many times, the POI that was closest according to absolute distance was not actually the closest after factoring in public transport and road routes. The other issue we ran into was that it made sense to go to the second-nearest hospital or grocery store in the event of a closure, but people would likely only go to one school or town hall. In those cases, we made it so that they had to go to their original schools/government buildings.

sections.heading: Finding inequality in the data
sections.text: We realized that we could repurpose leftover data we had collected from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to obtain interesting insights. For example, we used income data to realize that lower-income regions could be up to 3x more affected by infrastructure closure than higher-income regions.

sections.heading: Going from analysis to action
sections.text: The next step was figuring out how we could actually take action to resolve this gap. For that, we created a feature where we could test out how new infrastructure impacted people around. By taking the algorithm above and basically inverting it, we could figure out how the creation of, say, a new hospital decreased travel times and pressure on other local hospitals. We also created an algorithm that detected both: The most optimal spot for a new POI to decrease the average travel distance for everybody. The most optimal spot for a new POI to benefit lower-income regions. Interestingly, these two spots had extremely high overlap, providing tangible policy suggestions.

sections.heading: Natural language scenarios
sections.text: We realized that using UIs and manually assuming how infrastructure would react to extreme weather, natural disasters, and other events could be cumbersome. Thus, we decided it might be useful to have a natural language input so that people could test open-ended scenarios. For that, we integrated Grok and Gemini to take in a prompt, e.g. “There was an earthquake around Five Points station,” and apply the effects to nearby infrastructure. From there, our simulation would calculate the results and the AI would return both a summary of what happened and a visualization of what happened projected onto the map.

sections.heading: Handling disasters and imperfect data
sections.text: Another challenge that we faced was ensuring that the model could accurately represent what would happen if a natural disaster occurred. At first, the model would simply disable the incident point and only simulate based on this. To improve this, we adapted our simulation to increase the population in the surrounding area of the incident. This would simulate people evacuating from the disaster and make it more realistic. We also adapted the simulation to have higher pressure on hospitals during disasters to simulate real-life responses. Finally, an important flaw that was brought up was the lack of reliable public transport data. Although Atlanta’s public transport data is quite good, we couldn’t always expect such high-quality data, especially in regions where local governments can’t afford to spend resources on collecting data. Therefore, we decided to add a report feature where users could manually report train station data themselves and add it to our database.

sections.text: 🐙 Octavo: The Collective Memory Engine Get answers from people who solved it - Search through real human experience, not web pages

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We've all been there - asking Google "How do I break into product management from design?" and getting generic articles that don't capture the nuanced, lived experience of people who actually made that transition. Traditional search engines index static web pages, but the most valuable knowledge lives in human memory - the decisions, failures, and breakthroughs that shaped real careers and lives. What if we could search through collective human experience the same way we search the web? What if an AI could remember and learn from thousands of people's journeys, then provide wisdom that's impossible to Google? That's the vision behind Octavo - a search engine powered by collective memory that taps into the lived experiences of real people to answer questions that traditional search simply can't handle.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Octavo is a human-centered search engine powered by shared Letta memory agents that taps into the lived experiences of many to answer complex, nuanced questions better than Google ever could. Instead of indexing static web pages, Octavo creates a collective intelligence hive from real human memories and experiences. Core Innovation: Each user has their own Letta agent that stores their background, decisions, and life experiences like a personal journal. These individual memories are then anonymized and aggregated into specialized "sub-agents" for different domains (cs-careers, founder-journeys, grief-support, etc.), creating a searchable collective intelligence network. Key Features: 🧠 Crowdsourced Memory Responses : Get answers based on patterns from real people who've actually lived through similar situations - not generic blog posts or static content 🤖 Memory Agent Orchestration : Intelligent octopus-like system that automatically selects and coordinates the most relevant memory agents for each query 🎯 Auto Agent Selection : The system automatically identifies which collective memory domains (career transitions, startup journeys, etc.) are most relevant to your specific question 🔄 Version Control for Memory : Navigate through time with versioned memory branches - see "what worked for CS majors in 2020 vs 2024" or explore how advice has evolved 📊 Memory Exploration : Dive deep into the reasoning, tool calls, and specific memory blocks that power each answer with full transp

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Octavo combines three cutting-edge AI platforms to create something entirely new: 🗂️ Letta - Persistent Memory Agents Each user has their own Letta agent that stores personal experiences, decisions, and outcomes Memory blocks are anonymized and aggregated into domain-specific collective agents Persistent memory enables learning from patterns across thousands of experiences over time Version control for memory allows temporal queries and advice evolution tracking 🔄 Orkes - Intelligent Orchestration Complex workflows orchestrate multiple memory agents for cross-domain queries Parallel processing of memory retrieval, pattern recognition, and synthesis Dynamic agent selection based on query context and user needs Real-time workflow visualization shows the AI reasoning process ⚡ Groq - Lightning-Fast Inference Ultra-fast synthesis of memory patterns into coherent, actionable advice Real-time confidence scoring and pattern detection across memory blocks Dynamic response formatting based on query complexity and user context Sub-second processing of complex collective memory queries 🧠 Claude 4 - Advanced Reasoning Engine Powers our agents’ most complex thinking and synthesis tasks Excels at understanding nuance, abstract reasoning, and reflective summarization Enables emotionally intelligent advice and contextual awareness Seamlessly integrates with Letta’s memory to generate deeply human responses Tech Stack: Frontend : Next.js 14, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion Memory Laye

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Technical Challenges: Agent Coordination : Orchestrating multiple Letta agents with Orkes while maintaining response speed and coherence Temporal Consistency : Building version control for memory that allows meaningful temporal comparisons Collective Intelligence : Aggregating individual memories into collective wisdom without losing nuance Design Challenges: Trust Building : Users need to trust advice from "anonymous collective memory" - solved with transparency into reasoning and confidence scoring Query Complexity : Handling ambiguous, nuanced questions that don't have clear search parameters Integration Challenges: Multi-Platform Orchestration : Getting Letta, Orkes, and Groq to work seamlessly together Real-Time Processing : Maintaining sub-second response times while processing complex memory queries Scalability : Designing architecture that works for both hackathon demo and potential real-world deployment

devpost_page.title: Delphi
devpost_page.tagline: Voice-Driven Browsing for the Visually Impaired

sections.text: Delphi: Voice-Driven Browsing for the Visually Impaired

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Most of us take our laptops for granted. Google is always a few easy clicks away. But for some, these basic technologies are unfriendly and inaccessible. Our friend Moksh , who is blind, is one such person. For him, navigating the web is a maze of tabs and endless keyboard shortcuts to memorize. We witnessed his frustration listening for screen reader prompts and rebuilding his mental map of websites we take for granted every time the interface changed. Delphi was born from that moment: a promise to transform browsing into a conversation. An experience where every click and keystroke is controlled through your voice.

sections.heading: How it Works
sections.text: Delphi is a multi-agent network comprised of four unique AI agents that transforms any website into a seamless interface for voice-driven interaction. Voice Agent (Hermes) : This agent lives in our minimal web interface and converses with users. In addition to holding a friendly conversation, it identifies user’s intents in a browser and confirms actions aloud. Orchestrator (Zeus) : This agent identifies overarching tasks, maintains states, and delegates tasks between the other agents in the network. Vision Agent (Theia) : This agent uses computer vision to analyze screenshots, identify essential landmarks and UI elements, and describe what’s happening to the user. Browser Agent (Athena) : This agent takes action in a browser to execute the user’s goals through clicks, keystrokes, navigation, and more.

sections.heading: Technology
sections.text: Fetch.ai uAgents + Agentverse Google Gemini 2.0 Flash (regular and live) Browser-use Text-to-speech

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: Latency: Cutting round-trip time between screenshot, vision inference, and browser action. Error recovery: Detecting mis-clicks or failed navigations and auto-retrying with minimal user friction. UX tuning: Balancing verbosity vs. clarity in spoken feedback. Security & sandboxing: Preventing agents from executing unintended scripts or exposing sensitive data.

sections.heading: Accomplishments
sections.text: Achieved action recognition on complex pages. Modular design: each agent can be swapped out or upgraded independently. Decentralized architecture: multimodal agentic system on the Fetch network Persistence across multiple tasks Central orchestrator agent with memory and task queue

sections.heading: Lessons Learned
sections.text: The Power of Multimodal AI: combining vision, text, and voice to unlock unique workflows and enable innovation Agent Orchestration: having a central node with clear goals and autonomy Complexities of Accessibility: there isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution to accessibility — users have a variety of different needs that must be accommodated

devpost_page.tagline: A fairytale study buddy that lives on your screen, uses AI to see when you drift, roasts you in character, locks you down, and turns your breaks into games and study rooms with friends.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Once upon a time, a student sat down to study. They opened their notes, felt productive for about four minutes, and forty minutes later they were six videos deep into something they couldn’t explain and definitely weren’t going to be tested on. That student is every one of us. We’ve tried the usual fixes, and they don’t really work. Site blockers take two clicks to turn off. They also can’t tell the difference between actually reading your notes and staring at an “allowed” tab while your brain is somewhere else entirely. Studying alone gets lonely, too, and a “quick five-minute break” has a way of turning into the rest of the evening. We didn’t want to build a stricter warden. We wanted a study buddy: something that notices when you drift, actually cares whether you finish, and is a little bit dramatic about it. Fairytales already had the perfect cast. There’s a Wolf who’s always watching, and Cinderella’s clock, which strikes when time’s up. There’s a Witch who would absolutely turn your distracting tabs into toads. We pictured a storybook companion that could see your screen, react with real personality, and make both focusing and breaks feel like a story you’re in with your friends. That’s Once Upon a Focus.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Once Upon a Focus is a Chrome extension that gives you a fairytale sidekick on every page you visit. Pick one of eight characters (Red Riding Hood, Cinderella, the Wolf, the Duck, Humpty Dumpty, Poseidon, the Bat or the Witch), give it a name, tell it what you’re studying, and start a session. Your pet hangs out in the corner of your screen with a timer ring around it, cheering you on. Here’s where it gets fun. If you opt in, your pet uses Gemini to peek at your screen every so often and decide whether you’re actually working. Drift off and its mood goes from suspicious to annoyed to furious, and it roasts you, in character, about the exact video or page you’re on. Keep ignoring it and a storm rolls in over the page. To get out, you have to earn it: solve a riddle, pass a quiz Gemini writes about your study topic, type an oath backwards, or beat a challenge a friend sent you. If you really need out, holding Esc for five seconds always works. Your pet will sulk about it, though. It’s also a tutor. Turn on “look at my screen” and you can ask about whatever’s in front of you, whether that’s a diagram, an error message or a paragraph that makes zero sense, and Gemini answers from the screenshot. And it’s social. The Study Table shows which friends are studying right now, so you can nudge them or send a challenge that pops up in their next lockdown. In a Group Study Room, everyone shares one chat with a Gemini “Study Spirit” that answers the whole group and makes shared flashcards

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Once Upon a Focus is a Chrome Manifest V3 extension built with WXT, React 19 and TypeScript. The floating pet and the lockdown overlay live inside a Shadow DOM, basically a sealed-off bubble on the page, so they look the same on every site and never mess with the page underneath. A mood state machine with adjustable strictness controls how fast your pet loses its patience. The session timer runs on Chrome’s alarms, so it stays in sync across every open tab. Demo Mode speeds the timers up to seconds so we can show the whole experience live in a few minutes. Gemini is the heart of the project: it’s both the pet’s eyes and its social brain. For vision, we send a downscaled screenshot to Gemini Flash and ask for a structured JSON verdict: are you on task, how sure is it, what are you doing, and a “roast hook” that feeds the character’s next line. The same pipeline powers the “look at my screen” tutor. On the social side, Gemini runs the group study rooms, writes the flashcards, quizzes, riddles and friend challenges, and comes up with the Tavern icebreakers. Every call works its way down a list of Gemini models. If none of them answer, a hand-curated “offline storybook” takes over, so nothing ever dead-ends. The social features run on Firebase. Anonymous sign-in gives everyone an account with zero signup screens. Firestore holds friends, presence, nudges, challenges, study rooms, matchmaking and live games, all pushed to everyone in real time. Game moves run in Firestore transact

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Chrome extensions fought us the whole way. Our Firebase backend runs in a hidden page that Chrome provides for background work, and it turns out those pages can’t touch the extension’s storage at all. Nothing threw an error. Our social features just quietly didn’t work until we tracked it down. We fixed it with a small bridge that routes every storage read and write through the extension’s main background script and sends change notifications back. Then there was keeping Gemini alive on the free tier. Every model has its own small daily quota, and Demo Mode’s frequent screen checks chewed through our main model fast. At peak hours, some models would just hang, with no response and no error, and the tutor would give up and fall back to canned answers. So we rebuilt the AI layer. We also moved screen checks and roasts to lighter, faster models, which left the bigger ones free for real questions. The web itself had opinions too. devpost_page.tagline: a software platform that gamifies physical therapy, offering real-time feedback to help patients perform exercises correctly and effectively by combining interactive gaming with motion tracking.

sections.text: Inspiration As someone who has been doing research on spasticity and chronic pain relief for the past 3 years, I have talked to many patients who see physical therapists and are required to regularly exercise certain joints and muscles on their own as instructed by their therapist, to maintain a trajectory for speedy recovery. However, it is often difficult for patients to allocate time and stay consistent with these exercises. We’re all too familiar with life getting in the way of things, and in most cases, physical therapy is the easiest thing to push to the end of the priority list. But no matter how busy life gets, we’re never too busy to open up our favorite mobile game, scroll on instagram, hop on a late-night video game, or play a quick game of wordle. Thus, we thought that by combining gamification– an aspect of our lives that is becoming ever present in this digital age– with physical therapy, we can make rehabilitation more engaging, ensuring patients don’t stray from their recovery.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Thera_pixel offers two approaches to gamified physical therapy, one for younger and the other for older audiences. The first approach, Pizza Pursuit encourages patients to emulate upper extremity typically recommended by physical therapists to cook a pizza from rolling the dough all the way to cutting the slices. This game has a live video feed with ML pose detection accompanied by engaging and responsive pixel art visuals showcasing the pizza making process. Our second approach, Practice Studio, allows for patients to focus on perfecting the form and function for common physical therapy exercises, outfitted with real-time feedback to speed up or slow down the repetitions. Practice Studio is designed for older audiences to ensure they progressively overload their recovery safely and effectively.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built our project around the python CV2 library and Google’s MediaPipes 3d Pose Estimation tool, which allows us to determine relative positions of our joints in real time. Furthermore, we were able to analyze the accuracy of our movements using the IntelliRehabDS dataset, which we used to create ground truths progressions for the different movements.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One major challenge we faced was finding an effective methodology to create our ground truths. We deliberated between different approaches including exploring learned models and measuring progress by positive changes in key angle values. Both of those approaches did not yield effective nor accurate results. We settled on incorporating a timer telling the user when to start a given motion, then give feedback on pacing, as at each clock cycle, the angle of the user's arm is compared to the expected angle according to the data at a time t after the timer starts. this seemed to work relatively well, as we were able to set it to a pace that is easy to follow along with and analyze in real time.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Some big accomplishments we are proud of was our ability to take a novel, considerably small dataset and apply data science techniques like data cleaning and temporal interpolation to create consistent ground truth progressions for our desired movements.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Through the development of thera_pixel, we gained valuable insights into the intersection of gamification, physical therapy, and motion tracking. We learned that real-time feedback and engaging visuals can significantly enhance user adherence to physical therapy exercises. Additionally, working with a small dataset challenged us to implement creative data science techniques such as data cleaning and temporal interpolation to generate reliable ground truth progressions. We also discovered the importance of balancing precision with user-friendliness, as overly strict tracking could discourage users rather than motivate them.

sections.heading: What's next for thera_pixel
sections.text: Moving forward, we aim to refine and expand thera_pixel by improving the accuracy and adaptability of our motion tracking system. This includes training more sophisticated models that can better accommodate variations in user movement and different rehabilitation needs. We also plan to conduct user testing with both patients and physical therapists to gather feedback and tailor the experience for diverse demographics. Additionally, we envision expanding our library of gamified exercises, integrating more interactive elements, and possibly exploring augmented reality (AR) or virtual reality (VR) applications to further enhance engagement. Lastly, we will explore potential partnerships with healthcare providers to bring thera_pixel to real-world rehabilitation settings.

devpost_page.title: Echo
devpost_page.tagline: I often feel overwhelmed by life's changes, but this app reminds me: You're not alone, proven with data, private by design. It's safe to share today!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Has anyone here had a thought they were too ashamed to say out loud? Most of us have. And most of us believe we're the only one who's ever had it. Intrusive negative thoughts are near-universal — but they feel uniquely isolating. Existing mental health apps don't solve this. Therapy has a waitlist. Talking to friends feels like a burden. Generic affirmation apps feel hollow. AI chatbots feel clinical and impersonal. There's no app that just shows you, with evidence, that other people have felt exactly what you're feeling right now — and what actually helped them. That's what Echo is.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: You open Echo, tap the logo, and type what's on your mind. A few seconds later: "847 people have felt something like this." You scroll through their experiences — humanised, anonymised, real. Some of them found a way through, and left a note for you. No chatbot. No social feed. No clinical questionnaire. Just ambient proof that you're not alone. Core features: Thought submission — type or dictate a thought, submit it, and receive a count of how many others have felt the same, along with their humanised experiences as scrollable cards "What helped" — when users resolve a thought, they can optionally leave a note for others in the same situation. Shown verbatim, never paraphrased by AI — because misconstrued mental health advice is a real harm Breathing With Others — the home screen breathing animation responds to how many people shared thoughts in the same emotional space this week, creating a subtle sense of ambient co-presence Future You letters — after resolving a thought, users can write a short note to their future self, stored locally and resurfaced automatically if the same theme reappears Guardrails of Care — for risk-related themes (crisis, self-harm, etc.), a static safety resource block surfaces crisis helplines, rendered entirely client-side with zero logging

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Echo runs on a three-stage AI pipeline designed around a strict privacy constraint: raw thought text must never persist on any server, in any form. Stage 1 — Anonymisation The user's raw thought is sent over HTTPS to our FastAPI backend, where a self-hosted Qwen3.5-0.8B model (served via Ollama) strips personally identifiable information while preserving emotional specificity. "My boss FirstName at CompanyName undermines me" becomes "My [male name] at [tech company] undermines me." The raw text is discarded immediately — never written to disk, never logged. Stage 2 — Humanisation The anonymised text is passed to the NanoGPT API (qwen3.5-122b-a10b), which rewrites it as a natural, empathetic 50–60 word expression and classifies it into one of 30+ theme categories. This is the only form of the thought that ever leaves our server. Stage 3 — Semantic search The humanised text is embedded using sentence-transformers ( all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ) into a 384-dimensional vector and indexed in Elasticsearch. Cosine similarity search returns the closest matching thoughts from other users, paginated with search_after for efficient infinite scroll. The frontend is built in Next.js 16 with TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, mobile-first at 375px. Authentication is email and bcrypt only — no names, no DOB, nothing else. Personal history and raw thought text are stored exclusively in localStorage , client-side encrypted with AES-GCM, and never uploaded.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The hardest architectural decision was holding the privacy line at every step. It's easy to accidentally log a request body for debugging, or pass the wrong variable to an external API. We had to build middleware that explicitly blocks request body logging in all environments, enforce that the anonymiser is always the first service called, and verify that Elasticsearch documents contain zero user-identifying fields. Getting the breathing animation right was also harder than expected. The animation needed to feel emotionally meaningful — not just a spinner — and respond subtly to co-presence data without being distracting. We ended up with 9 layered SVG paths using Catmull-Rom interpolation, driven by requestAnimationFrame , with 5 distinct presence levels mapped from Elasticsearch weekly aggregate counts. The "what helped" verbatim storage decision created a constraint on the UX: we couldn't let AI touch resolution text after anonymisation. That meant designing a submission flow that felt natural while making it clear the user's words would be shown exactly as written.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: The privacy architecture is something we're genuinely proud of. We designed for the worst case: assume the entire infrastructure is breached. Even then — an attacker gets email addresses linked to emotional theme categories, and a dataset of humanised anonymous thoughts with zero user linkage. They cannot read what any individual wrote. They cannot link thoughts to people. That constraint shaped every decision we made. The count reveal moment works. Watching the number tick up to "847 people have felt this" — even in testing — lands differently than we expected. That's the thesis statement of the whole product made visible. The "what helped" flow is the feature we believe in most. The dataset grows every time someone gets better and decides to share it. The advice is specific, human, and unfiltered by AI. That specificity is the whole point.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building under a strict privacy constraint is a design superpower, not just a limitation. Every feature we couldn't build because of the privacy model forced us toward a better alternative. We couldn't store personal history on the server — so we built it client-side, which means it's actually private. We couldn't log sentiment trends per user — so we built aggregate counts per theme, which turned into the co-presence breathing feature. We also learned that the emotional design of a waiting state matters. The 2–3 second breathing animation during processing isn't wasted time — it's the moment users feel the weight of what they just shared. Shortening it or replacing it with a spinner would have been the wrong call.

sections.text: We want to
